opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the basic picture is something like this. There's a fairly robust empirical regularity where, if you increase the effective compute going into training, meaning raw compute times whatever multiplier you get from algorithmic improvements, you get pretty predictable gains in capability. Loss goes down smoothly, and downstream that tends to translate into models that can do harder and longer tasks.

The way I think about it, the important question isn't so much "does loss go down" but "what does an additional order of magnitude of effective compute buy you in terms of the things we actually care about?" One frame I find useful is to think about it in terms of the human-equivalent skill level or the time horizon of tasks the model can reliably complete. Historically, it seems like each few orders of magnitude of effective compute has gotten you something like going from a fairly dumb model to a model that's roughly comparable to a smart high schooler on many tasks, and then onward toward something more like a competent professional in narrow domains. And recently we've seen the length of tasks AIs can do autonomously growing quite quickly, doubling on something like a several-month timescale.

Then there's the question of what happens when you get to the point where AIs can meaningfully automate AI research itself. That's where I think the benefits of effective compute become especially important, because now additional compute isn't just making a better model, it's also giving you more and better AI researchers, which accelerates algorithmic progress, which increases effective compute further. So you can get this feedback loop. How strong that loop is depends a lot on things like how much you're bottlenecked on compute for experiments versus researcher labor, and I think there's real uncertainty there.

I'd also say there's a distinction between scaling pretraining and scaling things like RL and inference-time compute. A lot of the recent gains have come from the latter, and I think it's plausible those have somewhat different returns. But overall, my view is that the returns to effective compute have been pretty large and fairly reliable, and I don't see strong evidence that they're about to fall off a cliff. Combined with the fact that compute spending is going up very quickly, that's a big part of why I take relatively short timelines to very powerful AI seriously.

r001.rationale: The response discusses effective compute improving model capability and accelerating AI research, but it does not say compute can be directed among speed, capability, or parallel copies according to which yields the greatest benefit.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about this is that effective compute is sort of the thing that's been driving most of the progress we've seen in AI over the last decade or so. And by effective compute I mean not just the raw FLOPs you're throwing at training a model, but the combination of raw compute and algorithmic progress, where algorithmic improvements let you get the same capability for less compute. So you can kind of convert algorithmic progress into a compute-equivalent and then talk about the whole thing in one unit.

And the core empirical observation is that when you scale effective compute up, you get fairly predictable improvements in capabilities. The loss goes down on a smooth curve, and downstream, the models get better at basically everything, and in a way that's been pretty consistent across several orders of magnitude. If you look at the gap between, say, GPT-2 and GPT-4, that's something like three or four orders of magnitude of effective compute, and the difference in what those models can do is enormous.

So one way to frame the benefit is just: if you want more capable AI, historically the most reliable lever has been more effective compute. You don't need some brilliant conceptual breakthrough, you just need to scale, and you get a fairly steady return. That's actually a surprisingly unusual property for a technology. In most fields you can't just say "spend 10x more and get a predictably better result."

Now, I'd distinguish a couple of different things when thinking about the benefits. One is the direct capability gain per order of magnitude, which is the thing people usually focus on. My rough view is that each order of magnitude of effective compute has bought something like a qualitative jump in how capable the models feel. And I think there's maybe another couple of orders of magnitude of straightforward scaling available before you hit serious bottlenecks on power, chips, data, that kind of thing.

The second thing, which I think is underrated, is that more effective compute doesn't just let you train a smarter model, it also lets you run more inference. So if you have a given level of capability, having more compute means you can run many more copies, run them faster, let them think longer per task, do more search or best-of-n style approaches. And a lot of what matters for AI being transformative is not just how smart a single instance is but how much total cognitive labour you can deploy. So I'd say effective compute pays off twice: once in training and once in deployment.

And then the third piece is that compute feeds back into AI R&D itself. If you can use AIs to do a chunk of the research that improves algorithms, then effective compute scaling starts compounding, because algorithmic progress is itself a function of how much AI labour you can throw at the problem. That's the thing I'm most focused on when thinking about takeoff dynamics. Once AIs are substantially accelerating AI research, the relationship between hardware scaling and capability gains gets a lot steeper than the historical trend would suggest.

So to summarise: I understand the benefits as, first, you get reliable capability improvements per order of magnitude, probably with a few more orders of magnitude still to go; second, you get more total deployable AI labour from a given level of capability; and third, you potentially kick off a feedback loop where AI accelerates the algorithmic side, which is where I think the really big and somewhat scary dynamics come from.

r001.rationale: The response describes compute improving capability, speed, and the number of deployed copies, but does not say it can be directed toward whichever of those dimensions provides the greatest benefit.

astra-6.text:
I think the basic picture is that more effective compute lets you get more capable systems. By effective compute, I mean something like the amount of actual compute you’re using, adjusted for improvements in algorithms—so if you find a way to get the same performance with half as much compute, that’s effectively a doubling.

The benefits come through a few different channels. You can train a better model, you can make a given level of capability cheaper, and you can spend more compute at inference time to have the system work harder on a particular problem. Those aren’t perfectly interchangeable, but all of them can be useful.

And then the question is what those capabilities actually buy you. A particularly important possibility is accelerating research: helping people develop medicines, improve engineering designs, or do AI safety research. If you can automate substantial parts of that work, the benefits could be very large.

But I’d distinguish improvements in model performance from improvements in the world. You still need to deploy the systems usefully, verify their outputs, and deal with whatever bottlenecks remain. And scaling also increases the potential risks. So I don’t think ‘more effective compute’ automatically means a better outcome, even though it’s a powerful way to get more capability.

r001.rationale: The response describes using compute to train better models, reduce capability costs, or spend more at inference time. It does not state that compute can be allocated among AI speed, capability, or parallel copies according to which yields the greatest benefit.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the basic story is that if you spend more effective compute training an AI system, you can generally get a more capable system. By effective compute, I mean something that accounts for both the physical computation you’re using and improvements in algorithms—so you might get the same result with less compute because you’ve found a better way to train the model.

One benefit is that models get better at tasks they can already do: they make fewer mistakes, handle more complicated cases, and require less guidance. Another is that they become useful for tasks where the previous model wasn’t good enough to be worth using. That can make a relatively modest improvement in capability economically quite significant.

But I’d distinguish improvements in the training objective, which tend to be fairly predictable, from improvements in usefulness. You can predict that a larger training run will achieve a better loss without knowing exactly when it will become good enough to do some particular research task or reliably carry out a long project. Those downstream benefits are much harder to forecast.

r001.rationale: The response says more effective compute can produce a more capable system, but does not state that compute can be allocated among speed, capability, or parallel copies according to which provides the greatest benefit.
